generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, a search tool becomes precise when you control it. You join concepts with AND, group each concept's synonyms with OR, and hold phrases together with quotation marks. A wildcard on a word stem catches its different endings, and a date limiter keeps the results to recent work. These tools turn a flood of hits into a set you can actually read.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students taking the same keyword set into the search tool, and both run a search.

{{learner-a}} types all the words in one after another, with spaces between them. The tool returns tens of thousands of results, far too many to use, and the later pages go unread. The terms were there, but nothing told the tool how they fit together.

{{learner-b}} joins the terms with operators, grouping the synonyms with OR and the concepts with AND, and puts quotation marks around each phrase. A wildcard catches the word endings, and the result is a few hundred focused hits. A date limiter for recent years makes the set manageable.

Both used the same keywords. {{learner-b}} told the tool how they fit together, then refined from there.
generatedProse.summary: A search tool lets you control a search rather than just run it. You join concepts with AND, group synonyms with OR, hold phrases together with quotation marks, catch word endings with a wildcard, and narrow with limiters. When a search returns too much or too little, you refine it and run it again. You can now construct and refine a search of your own.

check.body: In the worked example, what did {{learner-b}} do to cut tens of thousands of results down to a usable set?

items.text: Combined the terms with operators and phrases, then added a date limiter.
Read further into the later pages of results.
Removed the keywords and searched the topic name alone.
Searched the same words again in a different order.
